newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: BER upbeat on S.African economy, interest rates.
newsitem.headline: BER upbeat on S.African economy, interest rates.

text.p: South Africa's influential University of Stellenbosch Bureau for Economic Research (BER) said on Wednesday it still expects two interest rates cuts this year and broader economic recovery by year-end, accelerating in 1998.

In a broadly upbeat assessment in its latest short-term forecast, BER said it expected growth of 3.1 percent this year, led by manufacturing and non-gold mining exports rather than by agriculture and consumption demand, which ought to make growth more sustainable.
Although high bank credit extension and growth in money supply had postponed moves to relax monetary policy, BER said it still expected a two percentage point cut in the bank rate this year.
This could be followed by another one, or even two, in the first half of 1998.

This was because strong export growth and sluggish demand for imports was expected to lead to a "substantial improvement" in the current account of the balance of payments. Combined with strong net capital inflows, liquidity was likely to increase in the domestic money market.
The major risks to the forecasts include a stronger rand and the indefinite postponement of monetary policy relaxation.
Although domestic demand conditions are expected to be relatively sluggish for most of this year, wholesalers and retailers are not experiencing sharp cutbacks in orders and sales.
This indicated a "soft" downswing and the economy could be near a lower turning point, BER said.

Non-gold export volumes grew at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate of more than 20 percent in the second half of 1996, with manufacturers reporting that favourable export sales continued in the first quarter of 1997.
BER said the manufacturing sector remained "strikingly optimistic" and was continuing its deep-rooted structural adjustment to become more outward looking.

"Given the more competitive rand and the improving and better synchronised demand conditions in the world economy, manufacturers could be well positioned to exploit export opportunities as they arise," BER said.
"Led by manufacturing and non-gold mining, the economic recovery should become broader based towards the end of 1997 and accelerate further during 1998," the report added.
In addition, inflation was expected to fall by two percent towards the end of the year while the foreign exchange market stabilised.

As the benefits of the export led recovery start to filter through in terms of more new jobs and greater personal disposable income, private consumption expenditure should revive towards the end of 1997 and through 1998.
"Lower interest rates and improving consumer confidence (bar unforseen shocks) should assist this trend," BER said.
Gross domestic fixed investment is also expected to show strong growth because of higher exports, infrastructural projects and large mineral-based projects.
